brief.head: Forty years in four
brief.text: Paul Graham, Amit Varma said, sees a startup as a me­dieval trad­ing voy­age: in­stead of work­ing at low in­ten­sity for forty years, work at high in­ten­sity for four. {102-C05}

brief.head: The pizza hypothesis
brief.text: Every busi­ness is a bun­dle of be­liefs, Ajay Shah said: buy atta and Italian tomato cans, sell pizza at a profit. Testing it teaches you how the world works. {102-C03}

brief.head: Beware the buzzword
brief.text: Peter Thiel, Amit Varma said, treats buzz­words in a pitch as a warn­ing sign: big data, cloud com­put­ing, blockchain, AI. A gen­uinely new idea doesn’t need one. {102-J07}

brief.head: Without Einstein
brief.text: If Einstein had not ex­isted, Shah asked, how long be­fore rel­a­tiv­ity? People would have got there bit by bit, but at a given mo­ment, one cre­ative fire mat­ters. {102-C10}

brief.head: Just chop the tree
brief.text: Abraham Lincoln, Varma said, would spend four of six hours sharp­en­ing the axe. Too many of us spend the first four thou­sand hours sharp­en­ing it. {102-J06}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah make the case for starting up
lead.head: Wanted: founders. Apply within

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 102

body: Amit Varma opened the episode by trans­lat­ing Bruce Springsteen lyrics into Hindi for Ajay Shah to iden­tify. Then, with “the tough part of the show” done, the hosts turned to their sub­ject: why ev­ery­one should start a busi­ness.
This was Part 1 of a two-parter, and the hosts dis­agreed on only one point: how hard to com­mit.
## The case for own­ing

Shah of­fered three rea­sons. The first was com­pe­tence: peo­ple work at a dif­fer­ent level when the work is theirs. He quoted James C. Scott’s *Seeing Like a State*: “the most pow­er­ful fer­til­izer is the ten­der gaze of an owner.” {102-C01}
His other two, that a busi­ness makes you a bet­ter em­ployee and teaches you how the world works, Varma called byprod­ucts rather than rea­sons.

Varma’s own rea­sons were about change. The usual script, he said, runs from a de­gree to one ca­reer track for thirty or forty years, “and then we re­tire, and then we get de­men­tia and then we die.”

Settle into one groove and you os­sify, he ar­gued, so that when the world changes no­body wants what you do. He cited Peter Thiel’s ad­vice to Mark Zuckerberg: in a rapidly chang­ing world, the big­gest risk is not chang­ing.
## All in, or de­tached?

Here the hosts parted ways. Shah favours side gigs run with de­tach­ment: low stakes, com­fort with fail­ure, many ex­per­i­ments. Traders who love money most, he noted, do less well, be­cause “their hunger and their need for the money is dis­tort­ing their clear think­ing”. {102-C06}

Varma called de­tach­ment a fine per­sonal phi­los­o­phy, but ar­gued that traders earn their calm by first plung­ing in with full pas­sion. To be­lieve a de­tached 30 per cent can beat some­one else’s 100 per cent is, he said, “al­most of­fen­sive” to those who throw them­selves in.
Shah said he as­sumed your 30 per cent al­ready re­flected full mas­tery. Someone else will have that mas­tery too, Varma replied, and give ev­ery­thing.
## Five rules for founders
The rest was Varma’s ad­vice, much of it drawn from founders’ clips on the Instagram ac­count StartUp Archive.
First, prize love over like. In Paul Graham’s for­mu­la­tion, a hun­dred peo­ple who love your prod­uct beat a mil­lion who like it. {102-C07}

Second, ig­nore naysay­ers. A 1989 test au­di­ence panned the *Seinfeld* pilot. Varma’s warn­ing: “the bet­ter your idea, the more likely it is that there will be many peo­ple telling you that it can­not be done.” {102-C08}
Third, start from in­side rather than hunt­ing for a gap in the mar­ket. Google began as an in­tel­lec­tual puz­zle called PageRank; Facebook started in a dorm room.
Fourth, focus. Sam Altman calls it a force mul­ti­plier, and Bill Gates and Warren Buffett both named it their most im­por­tant qual­ity. The hard part, Varma said, is say­ing no to things you love.
Fifth, act. “Action pro­duces in­for­ma­tion,” in the phrase of Brian Armstrong of Coinbase. Too many peo­ple never stop plan­ning.

Varma closed with Milan Kundera’s man in a fog, who makes his road one step at a time. Look back at him from a dis­tance, he said, and “you will see the man and you will see the road, but you will not see the fog.” {102-C13}
Everyone look­ing ahead is in fog, Varma said, and the only way through is to move for­ward. Start a busi­ness be­fore the next episode, he urged, and “I will be so happy.”

second.label: Focus
second.head: Buffett’s empty diary
second.deck: Amit Varma on what Bill Gates learnt from Warren Buffett

pic.caption: Warren Buffett speaking to University of Kansas business students in 2005

body: Asked in a joint in­ter­view to name their most im­por­tant qual­ity, Bill Gates and Warren Buffett gave the same an­swer, Amit Varma said: focus. {102-R22}

Gates, Varma said, had learnt from Buffett how to say no. Once he asked Buffett to set up an event. Buffett opened his cal­en­dar, and it was al­most blank. How did he do it, Gates asked. “I’ve learned to say no,” Buffett said. “You should also learn to say no.” {102-S08}

The les­son, Varma said, is not say­ing no to things you don’t want to do: even peo­ple pleasers man­age that. It is say­ing no to things you love, which Steve Jobs told the de­signer Jonathan Ive on re­join­ing Apple. {#ive}

quote.text: I’ve learned to say no. You should also learn to say no.

third.head: Leave A-B-C to anybody

pic.caption: Amit Varma on work only you can do

body: Amit Varma was chat­ting with a friend, a huge celebrity in the cre­ator econ­omy whom he would not name, when he broke down ev­ery­thing the friend does. {102-S07}

“A B C is stuff any­body can do. I don’t un­der­stand why you’re doing it,” Varma told him. D-E-F was what only the friend could do, like the Lucknow love story he had writ­ten, a film that is “so much him”.
Time is scarce, Varma said: longevity is great, but it is not im­mor­tal­ity. He is glad a show for a busi­ness chan­nel never worked out, since it was not some­thing only he and Ajay Shah could do.
Not that the door is shut. “Though if some­body comes with a shit ton of money, we are still open to it, but a shit ton of money only.” {102-J05}

p2.title: Start something
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s reasons to start, Amit Varma’s rules for starting, and the one point on which they disagree

quote.text: in a world that is chang­ing rapidly, the big­gest risk you can take is not chang­ing.
quote.who: Peter Thiel’s advice, as told by Amit Varma

box.title: Where the advice comes from
box.text: Much of Amit Varma’s ad­vice came from clips of founders and in­vestors on StartUp Archive, an Instagram ac­count he calls awe­some. Paul Graham, who started Y Combinator, re­curs through­out: love over like, com­press your work­ing life, just learn. {102-R09}

sections.label: Why start
sections.head: Owners tend better gardens
sections.caption: why everyone should start something
body: Everybody should take a crack at build­ing one or more busi­nesses, Ajay Shah said, es­pe­cially those who think their lives are tidy and de­fined: the cor­po­rate slave, the uni­ver­sity pro­fes­sor. A busi­ness can be any­thing from a side gig on Urban Company to a VC-funded firm aim­ing for an IPO.
His first rea­son was that own­er­ship raises your game, be­yond run­ning to some­body else’s KRA. As James C. Scott put it, the most pow­er­ful fer­tiliser is the ten­der gaze of an owner. {102-R02}

His sec­ond was that run­ning a busi­ness makes you a bet­ter em­ployee. His third was that every busi­ness is a set of hy­pothe­ses about the world, and test­ing them teaches you. “So you will do twenty five things that are wrong,” he said. “But out of all of that, you will learn.” {#wrong}
## Before you os­sify

Amit Varma called those two byprod­ucts rather than rea­sons. His first rea­son was that a sin­gle ca­reer track os­si­fies you, and when the world changes, no­body wants the one thing you can do. He read out lines from Benjamin Franklin and John A. Shedd against the com­fort zone. {102-J09}
His sec­ond was the pace of change it­self, in an age of AI and au­to­ma­tion. In Jack Welch’s words: change be­fore you have to. {102-J10}
~ Naval Ravikant, Varma said, pre­dicts that most com­pa­nies will be star­tups of four or ten peo­ple that scale to a bil­lion dol­lars. {102-R08}

quote.text: in a world that is chang­ing rapidly, the big­gest risk you can take is not chang­ing.
quote.who: Peter Thiel’s advice, as told by Amit Varma

sections.label: The quarrel
sections.head: Cool head or whole heart?
sections.caption: detachment versus full commitment
body: Everyone should start some­thing; the hosts dis­agreed about how. Ajay Shah, think­ing of peo­ple who al­ready have a main life, favours the side gig, where you nur­ture “lit­tle bub­bling fires” and ex­per­i­ment with them.
Detachment, he said, means the gig is not your all-consuming pas­sion and you are com­fort­able with fail­ure. Low stakes op­press you less, so you think more coolly.
Finance has a whis­per of this, he said: the traders who love money most do less well. {102-C06} He added that “if you’re a lit­tle de­tached, you’re play­ing chess, you’re play­ing a game”.
## Plunge first
Amit Varma was “com­pletely on with de­tach­ment as a per­sonal phi­los­o­phy”. But de­tached traders, he ar­gued, know trad­ing so well be­cause they once plunged into it with full pas­sion.
To think that a de­tached 30 per cent of your time can beat some­one else’s 100 per cent struck him as ar­ro­gance. {#thirty}

Shah replied that he as­sumed your 30 per cent al­ready re­flected full mas­tery. Someone else will have that mas­tery too, Varma said, and give ev­ery­thing. Even pod­cast­ing, once his side gig, be­came his main gig.
~ He could think of no one he knew who had built a suc­cess­ful busi­ness while being de­tached about it.

quote.text: I’m as­sum­ing that you’ve reached that level of knowl­edge where your thirty per­cent ac­tu­ally is full mas­tery of some­thing.

sections.label: Love over like
sections.head: Better loved than liked
sections.caption: love over like
body: Thinking about scale too early is dan­ger­ous, Amit Varma said. His first rule, put into words by Paul Graham, is that a hun­dred peo­ple who love your prod­uct beat a mil­lion who like it. {102-C07}

He learnt it on *The Seen and the Unseen*. He used to say he would rather have a hun­dred thou­sand peo­ple down­load an episode than ten mil­lion watch a YouTube show, where av­er­age view times can be fif­teen or twenty sec­onds.

When he checked, his av­er­age ses­sion was forty min­utes, and peo­ple lis­tened across mul­ti­ple ses­sions. “That is so off the charts that if you told me this fif­teen years ago when I was an in­ter­net pro­fes­sional, I would just have as­sumed you’re lying.” {102-S05}
## Slow down to please
Jan Koum, in an in­ter­view Varma thinks was with Sam Altman, ex­plained why early WhatsApp charged a dol­lar: “we didn’t want it to grow too fast.” {102-S02}
The team wanted users it could han­dle and please, with faster servers and more re­spon­sive cus­tomer ser­vice, be­fore going to the next stage. Varma found that “re­ally in­spir­ing”.
~ Get con­crete, he ad­vised: speak to your cus­tomers di­rectly and work on what they want. Too often, he said, we re­treat into num­bers and mar­kets.

quote.text: it’s bet­ter to be loved by a few than liked by many.

sections.label: Naysayers
sections.head: The trouble with ‘no, but’
sections.caption: ignoring the naysayers
body: Many peo­ple never take the leap, Amit Varma said, be­cause they lis­ten to scep­ti­cal voices. Whenever we hear some­thing new, our in­stinct is to say “no, but”. He con­sciously stops him­self be­fore re­spond­ing. {#nobut}

Customer focus groups, he said, are the worst way to test a new idea. The tele­phone was first imag­ined as a way for tele­graph op­er­a­tors to talk to each other, and even Silicon Valley’s media doubted the in­ter­net in the 1990s.
## Who to ig­nore
Think about naysay­ers that way, Varma urged: the bet­ter your idea, the more likely it is that many peo­ple will tell you it can­not be done. {102-C08}
Steve Jobs had utter con­tempt for con­sul­tants, he said, be­cause they have no skin in the game. {102-R15}

Vinod Khosla, the founder of Sun Microsystems turned ven­ture cap­i­tal­ist, once said that sev­enty per cent of VCs add neg­a­tive value to a com­pany. {#khosla} Unless you have lived through a founder’s daily crises, Varma said, you sim­ply don’t know.
~ A founder who has lived with an idea, kept awake by it at night, should take that con­vic­tion far more se­ri­ously than out­side ad­vice.

quote.text: hire the best peo­ple, and then ig­nore the freak­ing con­sul­tants be­cause they don’t have skin in the game.

sections.label: From inside
sections.head: Never mind the gap
sections.caption: starting from inside
body: “Whatever you do should come from in­side, not from out­side,” Amit Varma said. Hunting for a gap in the mar­ket sends you where ev­ery­one else is rush­ing, which is a path to medi­ocrity. {102-C09}
Instead, he cited Paul Graham’s ad­vice: just learn. Gain do­main ex­per­tise, and projects will emerge.

Most great com­pa­nies, he said, began as projects or hob­bies. Yahoo was a web di­rec­tory for Stanford. Page and Brin started with PageRank, a puz­zle about doing search bet­ter, and tried to sell it to other search en­gines. “They weren’t think­ing of a busi­ness at the time. They were think­ing of a pain point.” {102-S06}
## Only you

Peter Thiel’s rule is to work on some­thing that wouldn’t hap­pen with­out you. That need not mean Mars, Varma said: his long con­ver­sa­tions on *The Seen and the Unseen* would not exist with­out him. {#longform}

Ajay Shah ap­plied the rule by triage. After a bomb goes off at a cof­fee shop, first re­spon­ders sort peo­ple into green, who will sur­vive any­way, black, who will die, and red, where ef­fort counts most. {102-C11}
~ His lap­top is full of half-page scrib­bles, and he picks a few big bat­tles only he can fight. If you are doing what many oth­ers could, he said, you are prob­a­bly not del­e­gat­ing enough.

quote.text: The red is where you put the peak ef­fort be­cause your im­pact will be the high­est, your mar­ginal con­tri­bu­tion will be the high­est.

sections.label: Bias for action
sections.head: A road made step by step
sections.caption: the bias for action
body: The episode ended at the be­gin­ning, Amit Varma said: with start­ing. Life is a trade-off be­tween get­ting it done and get­ting it right, and too often we plan and plan and never start.
Brian Armstrong of Coinbase puts it in three words: ac­tion pro­duces in­for­ma­tion. Every time you do some­thing, you learn a lit­tle. {102-R26}
Kevin Systrom’s big­gest re­gret about Instagram, Varma said, was a pri­vate beta that ran for six months or so. The ad­vice: “Don’t do pri­vate beta. Just put your prod­uct out there.” {#beta}
## The man in the fog
Armstrong also pic­tured a foggy moun­tain: wait at the bot­tom for the fog to clear and you will be there for­ever. {#fog}
Varma won­dered whether he took it from Milan Kundera’s *Testaments Betrayed*, in which a man in a fog takes one step after an­other and, with each step, makes his road. {102-J14}
Seeing the past as a clearly mapped road, Varma said, is hind­sight bias. Certainty is some­thing you can only have when you look back; look­ing ahead, we are all in fog. {102-C13}
~ “So, dear lis­tener, have a bias for ac­tion,” he con­cluded. “Start your busi­ness.”

quote.text: when you’re look­ing ahead, we are all in fog, and the only way to nav­i­gate that fog is to move for­ward.

art.caption: Amit Varma on the bias for action

quote.text: So if you’re an en­tre­pre­neur with an idea, you’ve been liv­ing with that idea, it’s kept you awake at night, you’ve got to take your­self and your pas­sion much, much more se­ri­ously than ad­vice com­ing from out­side.

p3.title: Founders’ tales
p3.deck: Four stories Amit Varma told, and what each teaches a would-be founder

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how Airbnb’s founder served his first hosts
stories.head: Ding-dong, Airbnb calling
body: In the early days of Airbnb, when it had only a few cus­tomers, Brian Chesky went to see them him­self: what was each place like, and what was its owner ad­ver­tis­ing about it? {102-R10}
Amit Varma told the story to il­lus­trate Paul Graham’s rule that it is bet­ter to be loved by a few than liked by many. Chesky, he said, took those words to heart.

Chesky no­ticed that when hosts pho­tographed their own places, the pic­tures looked bad. So he asked one of them: would it help if there were a but­ton on the site that sent a pho­tog­ra­pher over to shoot the place? The host said yes.
A lit­tle while after leav­ing, Chesky called. “Hey, we’ve put a but­ton,” he said, in Varma’s telling. The host clicked it.

“And the next day the door­bell rings, the guy opens it, is Brian Chesky,” Varma said. The host was as­ton­ished: “Oh my God, you must be a re­ally small com­pany. Don’t you have any­thing bet­ter to do?” {102-S01}
Chesky him­self had landed up with a cam­era to take the pho­to­graphs.

It doesn’t mat­ter how many cus­tomers you have at the start, Varma said, if each of them loves you. Talk to each of them. Ask how you can im­prove things. If they want a fea­ture, build it just for them.
~ Once a hun­dred peo­ple love it, the prod­uct be­comes so good that it be­gins to spread, and then, he said, scal­ing isn’t dif­fi­cult.
stories.why: With only a few cus­tomers, a founder can serve each one per­son­ally and build ex­actly what they ask for. A hun­dred peo­ple who love the prod­uct will spread it, and then scal­ing is easy. {102-C07}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the founder at the door

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on an old British law for early cars
stories.head: Three men and a motor car
body: The first car, Amit Varma said, was not greeted as the fu­ture of hu­man­ity. It was seen as a toy for rich peo­ple, who would also hire a driver.
Early cars stopped after a cou­ple of min­utes, so each needed a stoker to start the en­gine again. Even the word, Varma noted, came from an older tech­nol­ogy.

Then Britain came up with the red flag law, which re­quired three peo­ple for every car. “One is a stoker who’s got to start the en­gine when it stops, not if. The sec­ond is the driver.” The third walked sixty me­tres ahead of the car, wav­ing a red flag so that horses and car­riages didn’t get into trou­ble. {102-S04}
~ Had Henry Ford sur­veyed cus­tomers, Varma said, peo­ple in trans­porta­tion would have asked for “bet­ter bred horses, faster horses”. {102-J11}

quote.text: So this is how out­landish the idea of driv­ing seemed.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the red flag law

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a test audience that got it badly wrong
stories.head: The pilot nobody wanted back
body: In 1989, a pilot of *Seinfeld* was shown to a test au­di­ence. Amit Varma told the story from a clip of Jerry Seinfeld him­self. {102-R12}

The ver­dicts were bru­tal. “One piece of feed­back I re­mem­ber was, No seg­ment of the au­di­ence wants to see the show again,” Varma said. Another said they didn’t like Jerry’s backup en­sem­ble, the cast Varma calls “the great­est”. {102-S03}
Had the mar­ket­ing peo­ple won the ar­gu­ment, the show would never have hap­pened. Luckily, some­one took the leap.

~ Varma asked Ajay Shah whether he had watched *Seinfeld*, then as­sured him that be­tween them they had watched it an av­er­age num­ber of times, since Varma had prob­a­bly watched it twice as much as the nor­mal per­son. {102-J04}
stories.why: Focus groups and mar­ket sur­veys judge the new against what al­ready ex­ists, so they tend to re­ject the gen­uinely new. The bet­ter your idea, Varma said, the more peo­ple will tell you it can­not be done. {102-C08}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Seinfeld pilot

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a founder who took a lesson from Intel
stories.head: All the chips in one basket
body: Drew Houston’s Dropbox reached an in­flec­tion point, Amit Varma said. It was build­ing video-sharing and file-sharing soft­ware, great prod­ucts both, and it was all over the place. {102-R24}

Then Houston read *Only the Paranoid Survive* by Andy Grove of Intel. Grove de­scribes how early Intel, far­ing poorly in a rel­a­tively sat­u­rated mar­ket for mem­ory chips, got the chance to make mi­cro­pro­ces­sors, and reached a sim­i­lar point. {102-R25}
The con­clu­sion, as Varma voiced it: “I need to focus. I need to go all in. I need to put all my chips in one bas­ket.” {102-S09}
~ Dropbox dropped the video side en­tirely, in­clud­ing, if Varma re­mem­bered cor­rectly, a cou­ple of com­pa­nies it had ac­quired for it.
stories.why: Focus can mean aban­don­ing good prod­ucts you have al­ready in­vested in. Many shiny ob­jects at­tract us, Varma said, but he is much more in favour of fig­ur­ing one thing out and get­ting that right.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Dropbox’s big bet

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 102. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Brian Chesky (Celeste Sloman, CC BY-SA 4.0); Warren Buffett (Mark Hirschey, CC BY-SA 2.0); Peter Thiel (Gage Skidmore, CC BY-SA 3.0); Milan Kundera (Elisa Cabot, CC BY-SA 3.0); James C. Scott (SOAS University of London, CC BY 3.0).

shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A labour of love about the mu­si­cian who mat­ters to both hosts, which Amit calls the show’s least-watched episode.

shelf.title: Seeing Like a State
shelf.creator: James C. Scott
shelf.why: Scott’s ac­count of how state schemes to im­prove the human con­di­tion fail when bu­reau­cra­cies can­not ‘see’ the so­ci­ety they rule, with a tool­kit (state leg­i­bil­ity, high mod­ernism, metis) you can apply al­most any­where.

shelf.title: Four Papers That Changed the World (Episode 41 of EIE)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts ex­plain land­mark pa­pers in plain lan­guage, no­tably Coase on why firms exist and Hayek on how prices co­or­di­nate a so­ci­ety no plan­ner can grasp.

shelf.title: The Nature of the Firm
shelf.creator: Ronald Coase
shelf.why: Coase’s an­swer to why firms exist when mar­kets can co­or­di­nate through prices: con­tract­ing is costly.

shelf.title: The Beauty of Finance (Episode 21 of EIE)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on why fi­nance ex­ists and why it mat­ters to the real econ­omy: fi­nance as ‘the brain of the economy’, not a casino for the rich, traced back to me­dieval trad­ing voy­ages.

shelf.title: StartUp Archive
shelf.why: An Instagram ac­count of founder and in­vestor ad­vice clips, the source of most of the ma­te­rial for the hosts’ episodes on start­ing a busi­ness; Amit counts many of these founders among today’s finest thinkers.

shelf.title: Mark Zuckerberg on Peter Thiel’s advice
shelf.creator: Mark Zuckerberg
shelf.why: Zuckerberg names Thiel’s line as the best ad­vice he got: in a rapidly chang­ing world, the big­gest risk is not chang­ing.

shelf.title: Naval Ravikant: ‘The future will be almost all startups’
shelf.creator: Naval Ravikant
shelf.why: Naval pre­dicts most com­pa­nies will be small star­tups of four or ten peo­ple that can scale to a bil­lion dol­lars, a fu­ture that re­wards nim­ble, en­tre­pre­neur­ial peo­ple.

shelf.title: Paul Graham on compressing your working life
shelf.creator: Paul Graham
shelf.why: Graham’s frame: in­stead of work­ing at low in­ten­sity for forty years, work at high in­ten­sity for four and give it ev­ery­thing.

shelf.title: Brian Chesky on Graham’s advice
shelf.creator: Brian Chesky
shelf.why: Chesky took Graham’s words to heart at early Airbnb, in­clud­ing per­son­ally pho­tograph­ing a host’s home.

shelf.title: Jan Koum on charging for WhatsApp
shelf.creator: Jan Koum
shelf.why: WhatsApp charged a dol­lar early on to keep growth in check while it learned to please its ex­ist­ing users.

shelf.title: Jerry Seinfeld on early naysayers
shelf.creator: Jerry Seinfeld
shelf.why: The source of the story about the bru­tal focus-group feed­back on the 1989 Seinfeld pilot.

shelf.title: Marc Andreeson on early naysayers
shelf.creator: Marc Andreeson
shelf.why: Andreeson ex­plains how in­no­va­tions we now take for granted, like the tele­phone, were first seen as cu­riosi­ties that would never go main­stream.

shelf.title: Bill Gates & David Letterman being skeptical about the internet
shelf.why: A fa­mous clip in which Letterman treats the in­ter­net as a mere cu­rios­ity while talk­ing to Gates.

shelf.title: Steve Jobs hates consultants
shelf.creator: Steve Jobs
shelf.why: Jobs’s rule was to hire the best peo­ple and ig­nore con­sul­tants, who have no skin in the game.

shelf.title: Vinod Khosla is skeptical of investors
shelf.creator: Vinod Khosla
shelf.why: Khosla, a founder turned VC, says sev­enty per­cent of VCs add neg­a­tive value, be­cause text­book ad­vice is no sub­sti­tute for hav­ing lived through a founder’s daily crises.

shelf.title: Peter Thiel says trends are overrated
shelf.creator: Peter Thiel
shelf.why: Thiel treats buzz­words in a pitch as a red flag.

shelf.title: Paul Graham says, Just Learn
shelf.creator: Paul Graham
shelf.why: Start by learn­ing and gain­ing do­main ex­per­tise, and projects worth build­ing will emerge from it.

shelf.title: Jim Goetz on pain points
shelf.creator: Jim Goetz
shelf.why: Supports the idea of start­ing from a real prob­lem rather than a hunt for a mar­ket.

shelf.title: Peter Thiel on working on problems that wouldn’t get solved without you
shelf.creator: Peter Thiel
shelf.why: Amit reads it as a fil­ter for scarce time: do what wouldn’t exist if you didn’t do it, at any scale, not just Mars mis­sions.

shelf.title: Sam Altman on focus
shelf.creator: Sam Altman
shelf.why: ‘Focus is a force mul­ti­plier on work’: work­ing on the right thing mat­ters more than work­ing many hours, and Altman has yet to meet a slow-moving per­son who is very suc­cess­ful.

shelf.title: Bill Gates and Warren Buffet on the best advice they got
shelf.creator: Bill Gates & Warren Buffett
shelf.why: Both name focus as their most im­por­tant qual­ity.

shelf.title: Jonathan Ive on saying no to things you love
shelf.creator: Jonathan Ive
shelf.why: Ive re­calls Jobs telling him, after Jobs re­turned to Apple, that you must learn to say no even to things you love and lose sleep over.

shelf.title: Drew Houston on focus
shelf.creator: Drew Houston
shelf.why: Houston de­scribes how Dropbox dropped its video-sharing work to focus on one thing.

shelf.title: Only the Paranoid Survive
shelf.creator: Andy Grove
shelf.why: Grove de­scribes Intel’s move from a crowded mem­ory-chip mar­ket to going all in, which is why it’s use­ful for any­one torn be­tween too many prod­uct lines.

shelf.title: ‘Action produces information’ — Brian Armstrong
shelf.creator: Brian Armstrong
shelf.why: Every ac­tion teaches you some­thing.

shelf.title: Kevin Systrom on a bias for action
shelf.creator: Kevin Systrom
shelf.why: Systrom’s big­gest re­gret was Instagram’s months-long pri­vate beta.

shelf.title: Testaments Betrayed
shelf.creator: Milan Kundera
shelf.why: Amit loves Kundera’s image of a man in a fog who makes his road step by step; look­ing back, ob­servers see the road but not the fog.

shelf.title: Life Lessons
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit and Ajay’s course on what they wish they had been taught at twenty: learn­ing how to learn, frame­works for think­ing, writ­ing, prob­a­bilis­tic in­tu­ition, eco­nom­ics, the his­tory of thought, per­sonal fi­nance (Ajay’s mod­ule is ‘legendary’) and health.

shelf.title: The Art of Clear Writing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ing course, which treats clear writ­ing as a test of clear think­ing.

laughs.text: Amit on quot­ing Bob Dylan’s ‘he not busy being born is busy dying’ so often that ‘even Dylan must be fed up’, be­fore an­nounc­ing he’ll find new quotes by look­ing ‘down into my iPad un­abashedly.’
Amit’s sum­mary of the stan­dard life script: ‘we be­come vice pres­i­dent, we be­come CEO, hope­fully, and then we re­tire, and then we get de­men­tia and then we die.’
Amit’s twist on Lincoln’s ‘Give me six hours to chop a tree and I’ll spend the first four sharp­en­ing the axe’: ‘Too many of us spend the first four thou­sand hours sharp­en­ing the axe.’

Amit’s anti-comfort-zone quotes: Benjamin Franklin’s ‘When you’re fin­ished chang­ing, you’re finished’, Neale Donald Walsch’s ‘Life be­gins at the end of your com­fort zone’, and John A. Shedd (‘with the dou­ble D’): ‘A ship in har­bor is safe, but that is not what ships are for.’ Amit notes that Ajay is a fan of ships, not of har­bours and safety.
Jack Welch: ‘Change be­fore you have to.’
